newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish insurance sector mergers seen - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Swedish insurance sector mergers seen - analysts.

text.p: Despite posting strong first quarter earnings on Tuesday, Swedish insurers are expected to continue wooing possible partners to secure their positions as international players.

"Restructuring and mergers are mostly taking place in Norway now, but then it's going to be Sweden's turn for domestic changes and further into the future we are likely to see cross-border activity," Nils Ringdal, analyst with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, told Reuters.
In early April, Norway's Christiania Bank and insurer Storebrand proposed to merge and Ringdal expects to see domestic Swedish mergers in 1998 and 1999.

Swedish insurers are rock solid at the moment, with Skandia on Tuesday reporting a 61 percent surge in operating profit to 1.48 billion crowns and Trygg-Hansa posting a 60 percent jump in pre-tax profit to 1.18 billion.
But analysts expect them to cast their eyes towards banks or rival insurers.

"If Skandia intends to go through with a listing of AFS (its assurance unit Assurance & Financial Services) it needs to merge its non-life insurance operations," Jonny Sylven, analyst at Swedbank, said.
Skandia is looking into a possible spin-off of AFS, which is prospering on the strong savings market while holding onto its non-life unit, that is facing fierce competition.
With AFS, Skandia is a world leading group with huge operations in the United States and Britain and it could very well thrive alone, analysts said.
"Skandia is doing very well on its own," Ringdal said. "It probably wants to merge with (Finnish rival) Pohjola, but it's not certain Pohjola is interested so I don't think that will happen."
Speculation has targeted such a merger for quite some time but Sylven also doubted the deal would go through.
But Trygg-Hansa, which is much smaller than Skandia and focuses on the Nordic market, could be in dire need of a bride in the future.

"Trygg-Hansa has tried to take over (Swedish insurer) Wasa a couple of times and still has the door open, but Wasa is not as interested because it is involved in cooperation with European insurance groups," Sylven said.
While Ringdal expected mergers between insurers and banks, Sylven saw insurers turning to each other.
"I don't think we will see banks and insurance companies merge as this doesn't benefit shareholders," Sylven said.
"There is not so much money to earn and not so large synergies as bank staffers are not trained to sell insurance and to train them is costly."

Instead Sylven expected insurers to attempt cutting costs by eventually ridding themselves of distribution channels. He saw them focusing on their succesful asset management and relying on independant insurance brokers working on commission.
Ringdal agreed that bank staffers would make poor insurance salesmen but found the problem easy to solve after a merger.

"Insurance companies could for example put their own employees in bank offices or they could sell insurance over the phone or through direct mail or they could make their products easier for bankers to deal with," he said.
